review.summary: A referral programme looks worth testing because, on typical assumptions, it adds about 17 customers and £61,719 in ARR for a total cost of about £10,972, roughly £640 per customer against £2,400 for paid acquisition. The absolute gains are small against a base of 3,000 customers, and every result rests on benchmark rates rather than your own data, so this should be a measured pilot, not a firm commitment.
review.lever: The figure that matters most is the share of referred people who sign up. Raising it from 15% to 20% adds about 5.7 customers and £20,644 in ARR, which is more than raising the referral rate (3.4 customers, £12,382) or the sign-up conversion rate (2.1 customers, £7,737).
risks: The refer, sign-up and conversion rates are preset benchmarks, not measured from your customers, so the real outcome could be well below the modelled 17 customers.
The £30,174 saving against paid channels assumes that the same customers would otherwise have been bought with paid spend at £2,400 each, which may not hold for every deal.

Monthly new customers only reach about 1.8 after the seventh month, so the first year brings in few customers, and the 18% churn reduction on referred customers is also an assumption that has not been tested.
actions: Run a 90-day pilot with a small group of existing customers to measure real referral, sign-up and conversion rates before committing the full £400 monthly running cost.
Set up referral tracking from day one so you can compare referred customers' churn and lifetime value with the rest of the base.
Test the reward level and the sign-up journey first, since a higher sign-up rate has the largest effect on results, and scale only if the measured figures beat the paid acquisition benchmark.
